title: Oral Communication and Presentation
unitGoal: Students will listen actively, contribute to discussion, organize ideas for speaking, use clear voice and body language, and present information respectfully.

lessons.title: Active Listening
lessons.learningGoal: Students will listen for main ideas, important details, and meaning before responding.
successCriteria: I can listen for the main idea and key details.
I can ask for clarification when something is unclear.
I can respond in a way that shows I understood the speaker.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise listening closely, checking meaning, and responding thoughtfully.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise listening closely, checking meaning, and responding thoughtfully.
lessonContent: Active listening means paying attention to what the speaker is saying and what the speaker means.
A careful listener listens for the main idea, not just a few separate words.
Important details help explain, prove, or support the main idea.
When something is unclear, a listener can ask a specific question.
A good response connects to what the speaker actually said.

studentActivity.title: Active Listening Mission
studentActivity.mission: Choose listening choices that help you understand and respond well.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: listening is active work
steps.text: Listening is more than staying quiet. A listener has to think about the speaker's main idea, notice important details, and decide what still needs to be clarified.

steps.title: Main Idea and Details
steps.prompt: Find the point first
steps.text: The main idea is the speaker's biggest point. Details are the examples, reasons, or facts that help explain that point.

steps.title: Listening Goal
steps.prompt: During a class talk about a science investigation, what is the strongest listening goal?
choices: understand the speaker's main point and the evidence used
copy as many exact words as possible into notes
think of a related story to share after the talk
steps.correctAnswer: understand the speaker's main point and the evidence used
steps.feedback: Correct. Listening should focus on meaning and support.
steps.hint: The best goal helps you understand the message.

steps.title: Main Idea
steps.prompt: A speaker says, 'Our group changed the amount of sunlight each plant received. The plant with steady sunlight grew the tallest.' What is the main idea?
choices: Sunlight affected the plant growth in the investigation.
The group measured plant height during science class.
The tallest plant received attention from the group.
steps.correctAnswer: Sunlight affected the plant growth in the investigation.
steps.feedback: Yes. That answer explains the speaker's main point.
steps.hint: Look for the idea the details support.

steps.title: Clarifying
steps.prompt: A speaker uses the term 'controlled variable,' and you are not sure what it means. Which question is most helpful?
choices: Could you explain which part stayed the same in your test?
Could you repeat your whole talk from the beginning?
Did your group enjoy doing the investigation?
steps.correctAnswer: Could you explain which part stayed the same in your test?
steps.feedback: Correct. The question targets the unclear idea.
steps.hint: A clarification question should be specific.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Active listening includes thinking about how details connect to the speaker's main idea.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Active listeners connect details to meaning.
steps.hint: Details are useful when they support an idea.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised listening for meaning.

steps.title: Show You Understood
steps.prompt: Respond to the speaker's idea
steps.text: A thoughtful response often summarizes, asks a follow-up question, or adds a related point. It should show that you heard the speaker before adding your own thinking.

steps.title: Best Response
steps.prompt: A classmate explains that a character changed because she learned to trust her friend. Which response best shows active listening?
choices: So your point is that the character's trust changed her choices later in the story.
That reminds me of a different book with a friendship problem.
I wrote about the setting because it was easier to describe.
steps.correctAnswer: So your point is that the character's trust changed her choices later in the story.
steps.feedback: Correct. It connects directly to the speaker's idea.
steps.hint: Choose the response that proves you heard the point.

steps.title: Helpful Notes
steps.prompt: Which note would be most useful while listening to a short presentation?
choices: main idea plus two details that support it
every date and number even if their purpose is unclear
questions to ask before the speaker gives the conclusion
steps.correctAnswer: main idea plus two details that support it
steps.feedback: Yes. Useful notes help you remember meaning.
steps.hint: Notes should help you respond later.

steps.title: Respectful Disagreement
steps.prompt: Which response respectfully disagrees with a speaker's conclusion?
choices: I understand your reason, but the paragraph gives different evidence.
I heard the topic, but I chose a different answer earlier.
The conclusion may need one more example before I agree with it.
steps.correctAnswer: I understand your reason, but the paragraph gives different evidence.
steps.feedback: Correct. It disagrees respectfully and gives a reason.
steps.hint: Respectful disagreement should connect to evidence.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A good response can include a question if the question builds on what the speaker said.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Follow-up questions can show careful listening.
steps.hint: Questions can be part of active listening.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised thoughtful listening responses.

questions.prompt: What should a listener usually find first?
choices: the speaker's main idea
the speaker's exact first sentence
the longest word the speaker used
questions.correctAnswer: the speaker's main idea
questions.reviewNote: The main idea helps the listener understand the message.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the idea that the class garden needs more watering?
choices: Several plants had dry soil by noon.
The garden has six rows of plants.
The watering can is stored near the door.
questions.correctAnswer: Several plants had dry soil by noon.
questions.reviewNote: Dry soil supports the need for watering.

questions.prompt: Which question asks for clarification?
choices: Could you explain what you mean by 'reliable source'?
Which colour did you use on your title page?
How long did it take you to finish the poster?
questions.correctAnswer: Could you explain what you mean by 'reliable source'?
questions.reviewNote: That question asks about an unclear term.

questions.prompt: Which notes would best help after a presentation?
choices: main idea, two supporting details, and one question
a list of side comments from nearby classmates
only the speaker's last sentence
questions.correctAnswer: main idea, two supporting details, and one question

questions.prompt: Which response shows the listener understood?
choices: Your main point is that the evidence changed your first prediction.
I noticed the chart during your presentation.
I was thinking about my own presentation topic.
questions.correctAnswer: Your main point is that the evidence changed your first prediction.

questions.prompt: Which response disagrees respectfully?
choices: I see your point, but the data table shows another pattern.
My answer is different from yours.
The topic has more than one possible detail.
questions.correctAnswer: I see your point, but the data table shows another pattern.

questions.prompt: Active listening means thinking about meaning while the speaker is talking.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: A listener should ask every question that comes to mind before the speaker finishes.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.reviewNote: A listener should choose helpful questions at a suitable time.

lessons.title: Asking Good Questions
lessons.learningGoal: Students will ask clear questions that deepen understanding and keep discussion focused.
successCriteria: I can ask questions that match the topic.
I can choose questions that ask for evidence, explanation, or clarification.
I can use follow-up questions to learn more.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise choosing questions that help a speaker explain, clarify, and support ideas.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise choosing questions that help a speaker explain, clarify, and support ideas.
lessonContent: Good questions help people understand a topic more deeply.
A clarifying question asks a speaker to explain something that is unclear.
A follow-up question connects to what the speaker already said.
Some questions ask for evidence or examples.
Strong questions stay connected to the topic and purpose.

studentActivity.title: Question Builder Mission
studentActivity.mission: Choose questions that help a discussion or presentation become clearer.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: questions have jobs
steps.text: A question can ask for a fact, an explanation, an example, evidence, or clarification. The strongest question depends on what you need to understand.

steps.title: Stay on Topic
steps.prompt: Useful questions connect
steps.text: A good question grows out of the presentation or discussion. It should help the speaker explain the idea, not move the group to a different subject.

steps.title: Clarifying Question
steps.prompt: A speaker says, 'The narrator is unreliable.' Which question best asks for clarification?
choices: What does unreliable mean in this part of the story?
Which page number has your favourite sentence?
Did you use a chart to plan your answer?
steps.correctAnswer: What does unreliable mean in this part of the story?
steps.feedback: Correct. It asks the speaker to explain the unclear term.
steps.hint: Clarifying questions target confusion.

steps.title: Evidence Question
steps.prompt: Which question asks a speaker to support an opinion with evidence?
choices: Which detail from the text made you think that?
How many slides did you include in your talk?
Would you choose the same topic next time?
steps.correctAnswer: Which detail from the text made you think that?
steps.feedback: Yes. It asks for evidence.
steps.hint: Evidence questions ask how the speaker knows.

steps.title: Topic Fit
steps.prompt: A student presents about how bees help plants. Which question best fits the topic?
choices: How does pollination help a plant make seeds?
How long did it take to decorate your poster?
Which animal topic will you study next month?
steps.correctAnswer: How does pollination help a plant make seeds?
steps.feedback: Correct. It stays with bees and plants.
steps.hint: Choose the question connected to the topic.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A helpful question can ask the speaker to explain an important word.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Important words sometimes need explanation.
steps.hint: Clarifying vocabulary can help everyone.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised matching questions to their purpose.

steps.title: Ask More Than One Kind
steps.prompt: Questions can go deeper
steps.text: Some questions need only a short answer. Other questions invite explanation, evidence, or comparison. Both can be useful, but deeper questions often help discussion grow.

steps.title: Open Question
steps.prompt: Which question would most likely lead to a deeper answer?
choices: Why do you think the author chose that ending?
What is the title of the story?
How many paragraphs did you read?
steps.correctAnswer: Why do you think the author chose that ending?
steps.feedback: Correct. It asks for thinking and explanation.
steps.hint: Open questions often begin with why or how.

steps.title: Follow-Up
steps.prompt: A speaker says, 'Our group changed our design after the first test.' Which follow-up question fits best?
choices: What did the first test show that made you change it?
What colour was the final design?
Did you finish before the other groups?
steps.correctAnswer: What did the first test show that made you change it?
steps.feedback: Yes. It builds on what the speaker said.
steps.hint: A follow-up connects to the previous answer.

steps.title: Compare Question
steps.prompt: Which question asks the speaker to compare ideas?
choices: How is this solution different from the one your group tried first?
Where did you put your conclusion on the display?
Which classmate read the introduction?
steps.correctAnswer: How is this solution different from the one your group tried first?
steps.feedback: Correct. It asks about similarities or differences.
steps.hint: Compare questions ask how ideas relate.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A question can be polite and still ask the speaker to explain evidence more clearly.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Respectful questions can be thoughtful and specific.
steps.hint: Good questions can be both kind and challenging.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised asking deeper questions.

questions.prompt: Which question asks for clarification?
choices: Could you explain what you mean by 'theme'?
Did you use three colours in your chart?
What did you name your project?
questions.correctAnswer: Could you explain what you mean by 'theme'?
questions.reviewNote: It asks the speaker to explain a meaning.

questions.prompt: Which question asks for evidence?
choices: Which sentence from the text supports your idea?
How long did you spend reading?
Which font did you choose for your title?
questions.correctAnswer: Which sentence from the text supports your idea?
questions.reviewNote: It asks for support from the text.

questions.prompt: A speaker says, 'The second strategy worked better.' Which follow-up question fits best?
choices: What made the second strategy work better?
Which strategy did you write down first?
Did your group use lined paper?
questions.correctAnswer: What made the second strategy work better?
questions.reviewNote: It asks for more about the speaker's point.

questions.prompt: A talk is about healthy sleep routines. Which question best fits?
choices: How can bedtime routines affect energy the next day?
Which colour is used on the sleep chart?
How many chairs are near the poster?
questions.correctAnswer: How can bedtime routines affect energy the next day?
questions.reviewNote: It matches the topic and invites explanation.

questions.prompt: Which question is most open-ended?
choices: How did the setting affect the character's choice?
What is the character's name?
How many chapters are in the book?
questions.correctAnswer: How did the setting affect the character's choice?

questions.prompt: Why might a listener ask a question after a presentation?
choices: to understand the speaker's idea more clearly
to change the presentation topic
to make the question time longer
questions.correctAnswer: to understand the speaker's idea more clearly

questions.prompt: A strong question can ask for an example.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: A follow-up question should connect to what the speaker just said.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.reviewNote: Follow-up questions build on previous ideas.

lessons.title: Speaking Clearly
lessons.learningGoal: Students will choose speaking habits that make ideas easier for an audience to hear and understand.
successCriteria: I can choose an appropriate volume and pace.
I can explain why clear pronunciation and pauses help listeners.
I can keep my spoken message focused on the purpose.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise decisions about volume, pace, pronunciation, pauses, and focused speaking.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise decisions about volume, pace, pronunciation, pauses, and focused speaking.
lessonContent: Clear speaking helps the audience follow the message.
Volume should be loud enough for the room without sounding forced.
Pace means how quickly or slowly a person speaks.
Pauses give listeners time to understand important ideas.
Clear speakers stay focused on the purpose and use words the audience can understand.

studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Volume, pace, pauses, pronunciation, audience fit, and focused messages

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity for guided speaking and listening decisions and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Clear Speaker Mission
studentActivity.mission: Choose speaking choices that help an audience understand a message.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: your voice guides listeners
steps.text: When you speak, your voice helps the audience follow your ideas. Volume, pace, pronunciation, and pauses all affect understanding.

steps.title: Choose for the Room
steps.prompt: Clear is the goal
steps.text: A speaker should adjust for the room, the audience, and the purpose. A small group discussion and a class presentation may need different volume and pace.

steps.title: Volume
steps.prompt: A student is presenting to the whole class. Which volume choice is strongest?
choices: speak loudly enough for the back row to hear without forcing the voice
use the same soft voice used for a partner conversation
raise the voice only when saying the final sentence
steps.correctAnswer: speak loudly enough for the back row to hear without forcing the voice
steps.feedback: Correct. Volume should fit the room.
steps.hint: Think about everyone in the audience.

steps.title: Pace
steps.prompt: A speaker notices classmates are missing important points. Which change would help most?
choices: slow down slightly and pause after key ideas
add more details without changing the pace
finish the talk and answer questions later
steps.correctAnswer: slow down slightly and pause after key ideas
steps.feedback: Yes. Pace and pauses help listeners follow.
steps.hint: The problem is understanding while listening.

steps.title: Pronunciation
steps.prompt: Why should a speaker practise difficult words before presenting?
choices: so listeners can understand important terms clearly
so the introduction has more formal wording
so the speaker can use fewer examples
steps.correctAnswer: so listeners can understand important terms clearly
steps.feedback: Correct. Practising words supports understanding.
steps.hint: Pronunciation affects meaning.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Pauses can help listeners understand an important idea.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Pauses give listeners time to think.
steps.hint: A pause can support meaning.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised voice choices.

steps.title: Keep the Message Focused
steps.prompt: Clear speaking needs clear thinking
steps.text: A strong speaker chooses details that fit the purpose. Extra details can be interesting, but they should not make the main point harder to follow.

steps.title: Focus
steps.prompt: A student gives a short talk about how to care for a class plant. Which detail best belongs?
choices: how much water the plant needs each week
where the plant pot was bought
which window has the best view of recess
steps.correctAnswer: how much water the plant needs each week
steps.feedback: Correct. It fits the purpose of plant care.
steps.hint: Choose the detail the audience needs.

steps.title: Audience Words
steps.prompt: Which sentence is clearest for Grade 5 classmates?
choices: The experiment showed that more sunlight helped the seedlings grow.
The data suggest phototropic response variation across specimens.
The thing with the plants changed because light was involved.
steps.correctAnswer: The experiment showed that more sunlight helped the seedlings grow.
steps.feedback: Yes. It is clear and precise for the audience.
steps.hint: Choose wording that is accurate and easy to follow.

steps.title: Transition
steps.prompt: Which phrase helps listeners follow a sequence?
choices: The next step is
Another interesting thing is
I also remembered
steps.correctAnswer: The next step is
steps.feedback: Correct. It signals order.
steps.hint: Transitions guide the audience.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A clear speaker chooses details that match the purpose of the talk.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Purpose guides the details.
steps.hint: Clear messages stay focused.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised clear speaking choices.

questions.prompt: Which volume choice fits a class presentation?
choices: loud enough for the audience to hear comfortably
soft enough that only nearby students hear
loud only when reading headings
questions.correctAnswer: loud enough for the audience to hear comfortably
questions.reviewNote: Volume should fit the audience and room.

questions.prompt: What should a speaker do if the audience looks confused during key points?
choices: slow down and pause after important ideas
add extra examples as quickly as possible
skip the next point to save time
questions.correctAnswer: slow down and pause after important ideas
questions.reviewNote: Pace and pauses can improve understanding.

questions.prompt: Why practise unfamiliar words before a talk?
choices: to say important words clearly
to avoid using examples
to make the talk sound more formal
questions.correctAnswer: to say important words clearly

questions.prompt: A talk explains how to use a class website. Which detail belongs?
choices: where to click to open the assignment
which browser icon looks best
how many students used the website last term
questions.correctAnswer: where to click to open the assignment
questions.reviewNote: It helps the audience use the website.

questions.prompt: Which wording is clearest for Grade 5 listeners?
choices: The character changes because he learns from his mistake.
The protagonist experiences a major developmental shift.
The person in the book becomes different somehow.
questions.correctAnswer: The character changes because he learns from his mistake.

questions.prompt: Which phrase helps listeners follow the order of steps?
choices: After that
Another thought
For a different reason
questions.correctAnswer: After that

questions.prompt: Speaking clearly includes choosing a suitable pace.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: A speaker should include every interesting fact even if it does not fit the purpose.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: False

lessons.title: Organizing a Short Talk
lessons.learningGoal: Students will organize a short talk with a clear opening, connected points, and a closing idea.
successCriteria: I can plan an opening that tells the topic and purpose.
I can arrange points in a logical order.
I can use a closing sentence that brings the talk together.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise planning short talks with logical order, transitions, and clear conclusions.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise planning short talks with logical order, transitions, and clear conclusions.
lessonContent: A short talk needs a clear beginning, middle, and ending.
The opening tells the audience the topic and purpose.
The middle gives main points with examples or evidence.
Transitions help listeners move from one idea to the next.
The closing reminds the audience of the most important idea.

studentActivity.title: Short Talk Organizer
studentActivity.mission: Choose strong ways to organize and connect ideas in a short talk.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: structure helps listeners
steps.text: A short talk is easier to follow when the speaker has a plan. The audience should know the topic, hear connected points, and understand the final message.

steps.title: Opening, Middle, Closing
steps.prompt: Every part has a job
steps.text: The opening introduces the topic. The middle explains the main points. The closing brings the ideas together.

steps.title: Opening
steps.prompt: Which opening is strongest for a talk about keeping a reading journal?
choices: Today I will explain how a reading journal helps readers track ideas.
A reading journal can be kept in many kinds of notebooks.
Reading journals are something we used last month.
steps.correctAnswer: Today I will explain how a reading journal helps readers track ideas.
steps.feedback: Correct. It states the topic and purpose.
steps.hint: A strong opening helps the audience know what to expect.

steps.title: Main Points
steps.prompt: A student's topic is 'three ways to prepare for a quiz.' Which set of main points fits best?
choices: review notes, practise sample questions, get supplies ready
choose materials, open notes, write a title
read a chapter, organize a binder, write a story
steps.correctAnswer: review notes, practise sample questions, get supplies ready
steps.feedback: Yes. All three points fit the topic.
steps.hint: Main points should work together.

steps.title: Logical Order
steps.prompt: Which order works best for explaining how to make a simple slideshow?
choices: choose topic, gather information, make slides, practise speaking
practise speaking, choose topic, make slides, gather information
make slides, gather information, practise speaking, choose topic
steps.correctAnswer: choose topic, gather information, make slides, practise speaking
steps.feedback: Correct. The steps are in a sensible order.
steps.hint: Think about what must happen first.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: An organized talk helps the audience follow the speaker's thinking.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Organization supports understanding.
steps.hint: Structure helps listeners.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised building a short talk structure.

steps.title: Use Transitions
steps.prompt: Guide the audience
steps.text: Transitions are words and phrases that show how ideas connect. They can show order, add another point, give an example, or signal a conclusion.

steps.title: Transition
steps.prompt: Which transition would best introduce a second reason?
choices: Another reason is
In conclusion
Before the topic begins
steps.correctAnswer: Another reason is
steps.feedback: Correct. It signals an added reason.
steps.hint: Look for a phrase that adds a point.

steps.title: Support
steps.prompt: A speaker says, 'Daily reading builds stamina.' Which sentence best supports the point?
choices: Reading a little each day can help students focus for longer texts.
Some books have chapter titles and page numbers.
Many people choose different places to read.
steps.correctAnswer: Reading a little each day can help students focus for longer texts.
steps.feedback: Yes. It explains how the point works.
steps.hint: Support should explain or prove the point.

steps.title: Closing
steps.prompt: Which closing best fits a talk about using a planner?
choices: A planner can help students remember tasks, manage time, and prepare for learning.
The planner has a calendar section near the front.
I used my planner yesterday and wrote homework in it.
steps.correctAnswer: A planner can help students remember tasks, manage time, and prepare for learning.
steps.feedback: Correct. It brings the main points together.
steps.hint: A closing should leave the main message.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Transitions can help listeners hear how one idea connects to the next.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Transitions guide listeners.
steps.hint: Transitions are guide words.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised connecting ideas in a short talk.

questions.prompt: Which opening clearly introduces a talk about safe online research?
choices: Today I will explain three habits that make online research safer.
Online research can happen on different devices.
My presentation has four slides and a title.
questions.correctAnswer: Today I will explain three habits that make online research safer.
questions.reviewNote: It names the topic and purpose.

questions.prompt: Which main points fit a talk about preparing for a field trip?
choices: check permission form, pack needed items, review behaviour expectations
choose lunch items, reread class notes, review a spelling list
open a laptop, write a paragraph, count supplies
questions.correctAnswer: check permission form, pack needed items, review behaviour expectations

questions.prompt: Which order best explains how to write a paragraph?
choices: choose idea, plan details, draft, revise
draft, revise, choose idea, plan details
revise, plan details, draft, choose idea
questions.correctAnswer: choose idea, plan details, draft, revise

questions.prompt: Which phrase adds another point?
choices: In addition
To sum up
Before the topic
questions.correctAnswer: In addition

questions.prompt: Which sentence supports the point 'A checklist helps teamwork'?
choices: It lets group members see which jobs are finished and which still need work.
A checklist can be written on paper or typed on a screen.
Some checklists use boxes beside each line.
questions.correctAnswer: It lets group members see which jobs are finished and which still need work.
questions.reviewNote: It explains why the checklist helps.

questions.prompt: Which closing fits a talk about choosing reliable sources?
choices: Reliable sources help readers trust that information has been checked.
Some websites use menus at the top of the page.
I found three websites during research time.
questions.correctAnswer: Reliable sources help readers trust that information has been checked.

questions.prompt: A short talk should have connected points instead of unrelated facts.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: The closing should help the audience remember the main idea.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.reviewNote: A closing brings the talk together.

lessons.title: Using Voice and Body Language
lessons.learningGoal: Students will explain how voice, posture, gestures, and eye contact support a spoken message.
successCriteria: I can match voice choices to the purpose of a message.
I can choose body language that helps the audience listen.
I can identify gestures or movement that support meaning.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise choosing voice and body language that supports meaning without distracting from the message.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise choosing voice and body language that supports meaning without distracting from the message.
lessonContent: Voice and body language are part of oral communication.
Tone and expression help show the feeling or purpose of a message.
Posture and eye contact can show confidence and respect for the audience.
Gestures should support the message instead of distracting from it.
Different purposes may call for different voice and body choices.

studentActivityPlan.title: Voice and Body Language Mission
studentActivityPlan.description: Choose presentation choices that support the spoken message.
studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.title: Using Voice and Body Language Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Tone, expression, posture, eye contact, gesture, and audience support

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity for guided speaking and listening decisions and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Voice and Body Language Mission
studentActivity.mission: Choose presentation choices that support the spoken message.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: voice carries meaning
steps.text: The same words can sound different depending on tone, expression, pace, and volume. Voice choices should match the purpose and audience.

steps.title: Match the Purpose
steps.prompt: Use voice intentionally
steps.text: A safety announcement, a story reading, and a research presentation do not need exactly the same voice. The speaker should choose a tone that fits the message.

steps.title: Tone
steps.prompt: Which tone best fits a reminder about careful hallway movement?
choices: calm and serious
excited and dramatic
quiet and uncertain
steps.correctAnswer: calm and serious
steps.feedback: Correct. The tone matches a safety reminder.
steps.hint: Think about the purpose of the message.

steps.title: Expression
steps.prompt: A student reads a funny moment from a story. Which choice would help the audience understand the mood?
choices: use light expression while still reading clearly
use the same flat voice for every sentence
rush through the sentence before explaining it
steps.correctAnswer: use light expression while still reading clearly
steps.feedback: Yes. Expression can support mood.
steps.hint: Voice can show feeling without losing clarity.

steps.title: Emphasis
steps.prompt: A speaker wants listeners to remember one key word. What voice choice could help?
choices: pause briefly before the key word and say it clearly
make every word sound equally important
add a new detail right after the key word
steps.correctAnswer: pause briefly before the key word and say it clearly
steps.feedback: Correct. A pause and clear voice can create emphasis.
steps.hint: Emphasis shows importance.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Tone can change how listeners understand a spoken message.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Tone affects meaning.
steps.hint: Voice choices communicate.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised matching voice to meaning.

steps.title: Support the Message
steps.prompt: Body language should help
steps.text: Posture, eye contact, gestures, and movement can help the audience follow a presentation. The goal is to support the message, not take attention away from it.

steps.title: Posture
steps.prompt: Which body language choice best supports a class presentation?
choices: stand in a balanced way and face the audience
turn toward the screen for most of the talk
shift position each time a new sentence begins
steps.correctAnswer: stand in a balanced way and face the audience
steps.feedback: Correct. It helps the audience listen.
steps.hint: Body language should make communication easier.

steps.title: Gesture
steps.prompt: A speaker explains three steps in a process. Which gesture would support the message?
choices: show one, two, and three with fingers as each step is named
tap the notes each time a word is read
point to different parts of the room between steps
steps.correctAnswer: show one, two, and three with fingers as each step is named
steps.feedback: Yes. The gesture matches the structure.
steps.hint: Gestures should connect to meaning.

steps.title: Eye Contact
steps.prompt: What is a good way to use eye contact during a presentation?
choices: look up from notes regularly to include different parts of the audience
look only at the first row to stay focused
read every sentence from notes before looking up
steps.correctAnswer: look up from notes regularly to include different parts of the audience
steps.feedback: Correct. It helps connect with the audience.
steps.hint: Eye contact can be brief and natural.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Gestures are most helpful when they support what the speaker is saying.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Gestures should fit the message.
steps.hint: Useful gestures add meaning.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised voice and body language choices.

quiz.title: Using Voice and Body Language Quiz

questions.prompt: Which tone best fits a report about a science result?
choices: clear and thoughtful
playful and exaggerated
uncertain and barely audible
questions.correctAnswer: clear and thoughtful
questions.reviewNote: The tone fits an informational report.

questions.prompt: Why use expression when reading part of a story aloud?
choices: to help listeners understand the mood and speaker
to make the reading sound longer
to replace the need to understand the words
questions.correctAnswer: to help listeners understand the mood and speaker

questions.prompt: How can a speaker emphasize an important point?
choices: pause before it and say it clearly
add several extra points right after it
look down while saying it
questions.correctAnswer: pause before it and say it clearly
questions.reviewNote: A pause can help important ideas stand out.

questions.prompt: Which posture helps during a presentation?
choices: balanced and facing the audience
turned away while reading slides
leaning over notes for most of the talk
questions.correctAnswer: balanced and facing the audience

questions.prompt: Which gesture best supports directions with three steps?
choices: briefly count the steps with fingers
move the hands the same way for each sentence
hold the paper higher during the conclusion
questions.correctAnswer: briefly count the steps with fingers

questions.prompt: Which eye contact choice is strongest?
choices: look up regularly and include different parts of the audience
look at one friend for the whole talk
look only at the notes until question time
questions.correctAnswer: look up regularly and include different parts of the audience

questions.prompt: Body language can support or weaken a spoken message.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: The same tone is best for every speaking purpose.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: False

lessons.title: Group Discussion Skills
lessons.learningGoal: Students will contribute to group discussions by listening, building on ideas, and sharing respectfully.
successCriteria: I can add an idea that connects to the discussion.
I can build on another person's idea with a reason or example.
I can help a group stay respectful and focused.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise discussion choices that keep group work focused, respectful, and useful.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise discussion choices that keep group work focused, respectful, and useful.
lessonContent: A group discussion works best when members listen and contribute.
A contribution should connect to the topic or task.
Building on an idea means adding a reason, example, question, or connection.
Turn-taking helps more voices be heard.
Respectful discussion can include different opinions when people use reasons and listen well.
practiceIdeas: Share the student mission for practice stars.
Use the lesson quiz as a scored oral communication check.
Review missed questions before assigning the next Oral Communication and Presentation lesson.

studentActivityPlan.title: Discussion Team Mission
studentActivityPlan.description: Choose discussion moves that help a group think and work together.
studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.title: Group Discussion Skills Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Topic fit, building on ideas, turn-taking, respectful disagreement, and group focus

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity for guided speaking and listening decisions and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Discussion Team Mission
studentActivity.mission: Choose discussion moves that help a group think and work together.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: discussion is shared work
steps.text: In a discussion, the goal is not only to say something. The goal is to help the group understand the topic, solve a problem, or make a thoughtful decision.

steps.title: Connect to the Topic
steps.prompt: Useful contributions fit
steps.text: A strong contribution connects to the question or task. It can add a reason, example, question, or careful disagreement.

steps.title: Topic Fit
steps.prompt: A group is discussing which source is best for a research project. Which comment best fits?
choices: The official museum page has dates and author information, so it may be reliable.
I found a website with a bright homepage and many pictures.
Our group should decide who will print the final copy.
steps.correctAnswer: The official museum page has dates and author information, so it may be reliable.
steps.feedback: Correct. It fits the discussion and gives a reason.
steps.hint: Choose the comment that helps the group think about sources.

steps.title: Add a Reason
steps.prompt: A student says, 'I think paragraph two is the strongest.' Which addition would help most?
choices: It gives two examples that support the topic sentence.
It is near the middle of the page.
It was the paragraph I read first.
steps.correctAnswer: It gives two examples that support the topic sentence.
steps.feedback: Yes. It gives a useful reason.
steps.hint: A reason should explain the thinking.

steps.title: Question Move
steps.prompt: Which question would help a group choose evidence for an answer?
choices: Which detail best proves our main point?
Who wants to read the next paragraph aloud?
How much space is left on the poster?
steps.correctAnswer: Which detail best proves our main point?
steps.feedback: Correct. It focuses on evidence.
steps.hint: Evidence questions help academic discussion.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A discussion contribution should connect to the group's topic or task.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Topic fit matters.
steps.hint: Connected ideas help the group.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised clear discussion contributions.

steps.title: Build on Ideas
steps.prompt: Use what others say
steps.text: Building on someone else's idea shows listening. You might add an example, compare ideas, ask a follow-up question, or offer a reasoned disagreement.

steps.title: Build On
steps.prompt: A classmate says, 'The character seems nervous.' Which response builds on that idea?
choices: Yes, and the repeated short sentences show how rushed her thoughts are.
I chose a different character for my answer.
The chapter also has a setting description.
steps.correctAnswer: Yes, and the repeated short sentences show how rushed her thoughts are.
steps.feedback: Correct. It adds evidence to the idea.
steps.hint: Build by adding support or connection.

steps.title: Turn-Taking
steps.prompt: Two students have spoken several times, and one student has not shared yet. Which group move is strongest?
choices: invite the student to share if they would like to add an idea
continue with the speakers who have the most prepared notes
switch to writing so the group can finish faster
steps.correctAnswer: invite the student to share if they would like to add an idea
steps.feedback: Yes. It makes room without forcing.
steps.hint: Good discussion includes others respectfully.

steps.title: Respectful Difference
steps.prompt: Which sentence gives a different opinion respectfully?
choices: I see the evidence differently because the last paragraph changes the meaning.
That answer is not the one our group should use.
My idea has more details, so it should go first.
steps.correctAnswer: I see the evidence differently because the last paragraph changes the meaning.
steps.feedback: Correct. It gives a reason and stays respectful.
steps.hint: Different opinions should include reasons.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A group can disagree respectfully when members explain their reasons and listen.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Respectful disagreement can improve thinking.
steps.hint: Discussion is not only agreement.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised building ideas together.

questions.prompt: A group is choosing evidence for a reading response. Which comment fits best?
choices: This sentence supports our answer because it shows the character's motive.
The book cover uses dark colours.
We should decide who writes the title.
questions.correctAnswer: This sentence supports our answer because it shows the character's motive.

questions.prompt: Which contribution includes a reason?
choices: I think the first source is better because it lists the author and date.
I found the first source before the second one.
The first source has a longer title.
questions.correctAnswer: I think the first source is better because it lists the author and date.

questions.prompt: Which question helps a group check its answer?
choices: Does our evidence match the question we were asked?
Who has the neatest handwriting?
Which paragraph is closest to the top?
questions.correctAnswer: Does our evidence match the question we were asked?
questions.reviewNote: It checks the quality of the answer.

questions.prompt: Which sentence builds on a classmate's idea?
choices: I agree, and the chart gives another example of that pattern.
I also have a different idea about the next topic.
I remember seeing a chart in another book.
questions.correctAnswer: I agree, and the chart gives another example of that pattern.

questions.prompt: What helps a group hear more voices?
choices: make space for students who have not shared yet
let the fastest speaker lead each answer
choose one person to answer every question
questions.correctAnswer: make space for students who have not shared yet

questions.prompt: Which disagreement is respectful and useful?
choices: I read that sentence differently because it describes the opposite effect.
I do not think that answer should count.
Our group already has enough ideas.
questions.correctAnswer: I read that sentence differently because it describes the opposite effect.

questions.prompt: Building on an idea can include adding evidence or an example.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.reviewNote: That is one way to build.

questions.prompt: A group discussion should stay connected to the task.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

lessons.title: Giving and Receiving Feedback
lessons.learningGoal: Students will give and receive feedback that is specific, respectful, and useful for revision.
successCriteria: I can identify feedback that is specific and helpful.
I can give feedback that names a strength and a next step.
I can use feedback to decide what to revise.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise recognizing helpful feedback and using it to improve speaking or writing.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise recognizing helpful feedback and using it to improve speaking or writing.
lessonContent: Feedback is information that helps a learner improve.
Helpful feedback is specific, respectful, and connected to the goal.
A strength names something that is already working.
A next step suggests one useful improvement.
Receiving feedback well means considering it and deciding what revision would help.
practiceIdeas: Share the student mission for practice stars.
Use the lesson quiz as a scored oral communication check.
Review missed questions before assigning the next Oral Communication and Presentation lesson.

studentActivityPlan.title: Helpful Feedback Mission
studentActivityPlan.description: Choose feedback that helps a speaker or writer improve.
studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.title: Giving and Receiving Feedback Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Specific feedback, strengths, next steps, revision choices, and respectful response

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity for guided speaking and listening decisions and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Helpful Feedback Mission
studentActivity.mission: Choose feedback that helps a speaker or writer improve.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: feedback should help
steps.text: Feedback is useful when it helps someone understand what is working and what could improve. It should be specific enough to guide the next revision.

steps.title: Strength and Next Step
steps.prompt: Name what works and what to try next
steps.text: Good feedback often includes a strength and a next step. The strength tells what to keep. The next step tells what to revise.

steps.title: Specific Feedback
steps.prompt: Which feedback is most useful after a short talk?
choices: Your opening clearly tells the topic; add one example to support your second point.
Your talk was interesting and had a good topic.
You should make the middle part better.
steps.correctAnswer: Your opening clearly tells the topic; add one example to support your second point.
steps.feedback: Correct. It names a strength and a specific next step.
steps.hint: Useful feedback gives clear information.

steps.title: Strength
steps.prompt: Which comment names a clear strength?
choices: Your voice was easy to hear from the back of the room.
Your presentation had several parts.
You finished close to the time limit.
steps.correctAnswer: Your voice was easy to hear from the back of the room.
steps.feedback: Yes. It names a clear speaking strength.
steps.hint: A strength says what worked well.

steps.title: Next Step
steps.prompt: A student's presentation has good facts but no closing sentence. Which next step fits best?
choices: Add a closing sentence that reminds listeners of the main idea.
Use a larger title on the first slide.
Practise saying the first sentence more slowly.
steps.correctAnswer: Add a closing sentence that reminds listeners of the main idea.
steps.feedback: Correct. It matches the need.
steps.hint: The next step should solve the problem.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Helpful feedback should connect to the assignment goal.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Feedback should match the goal.
steps.hint: Goal-connected feedback is easier to use.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised spotting helpful feedback.

steps.title: Decide What to Revise
steps.prompt: Feedback is a tool
steps.text: You do not need to change everything at once. A learner should look for the feedback that best matches the goal and choose a clear revision step.

steps.title: Revision Choice
steps.prompt: Feedback says, 'Your examples are strong, but your main point is not clear until the end.' What revision fits best?
choices: Move the main point into the opening and keep the examples.
Replace the examples with shorter sentences.
Add a new picture before each example.
steps.correctAnswer: Move the main point into the opening and keep the examples.
steps.feedback: Correct. It keeps the strength and fixes the issue.
steps.hint: Use the feedback to guide one helpful change.

steps.title: Receiving Feedback
steps.prompt: Which response shows a student is using feedback well?
choices: I will check whether my second point needs clearer evidence.
I will revise the whole presentation before checking the goal.
I will keep the presentation the same because it is finished.
steps.correctAnswer: I will check whether my second point needs clearer evidence.
steps.feedback: Yes. It considers a specific improvement.
steps.hint: Good response focuses on revision.

steps.title: Peer Feedback
steps.prompt: Which peer feedback would best help a classmate improve a visual aid?
choices: The chart supports your point, but the labels need to be easier to read.
The chart is my favourite part of the whole presentation.
The chart has lines, labels, and two colours.
steps.correctAnswer: The chart supports your point, but the labels need to be easier to read.
steps.feedback: Correct. It names what works and what to fix.
steps.hint: Specific feedback helps revision.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Receiving feedback well means thinking about it before deciding what to revise.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Feedback needs thoughtful use.
steps.hint: Feedback is considered, not copied without thought.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised giving and using feedback.

questions.prompt: Which feedback is most specific?
choices: Your second reason is clear; add evidence from the article to support it.
Your work is good and easy to read.
You should improve the answer a bit.
questions.correctAnswer: Your second reason is clear; add evidence from the article to support it.
questions.reviewNote: It gives a clear strength and next step.

questions.prompt: Which comment names a strength?
choices: Your conclusion connects back to the main idea.
Your paragraph is about the topic.
Your work has a title and sentences.
questions.correctAnswer: Your conclusion connects back to the main idea.

questions.prompt: A talk has strong facts but no order. Which next step fits best?
choices: Put the facts into an order that helps listeners follow.
Choose a different topic for the talk.
Read the final sentence with more expression.
questions.correctAnswer: Put the facts into an order that helps listeners follow.

questions.prompt: Feedback says, 'Your voice is clear, but your visual has too much small text.' What should the student revise?
choices: make the visual easier to read
change the speaking voice completely
add more facts to the visual
questions.correctAnswer: make the visual easier to read

questions.prompt: Which response to feedback is most useful?
choices: I will decide which suggestion best helps my goal.
I will change whatever my partner mentions first.
I will focus only on the positive comment.
questions.correctAnswer: I will decide which suggestion best helps my goal.
questions.reviewNote: The student thinks about the goal.

questions.prompt: Which feedback helps improve a poster?
choices: Your headings are clear; make the date easier to find.
Your poster uses a clear title and one image.
Your topic is one many students know.
questions.correctAnswer: Your headings are clear; make the date easier to find.
questions.reviewNote: It gives a useful next step.

questions.prompt: Helpful feedback is specific, respectful, and connected to the goal.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: A next step should help the learner know what to try next.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

lessons.title: Preparing a Presentation
lessons.learningGoal: Students will prepare a presentation by planning audience, purpose, content, visuals, practice, and final checks.
successCriteria: I can plan a presentation for a clear audience and purpose.
I can choose notes and visuals that support the message.
I can practise and revise before presenting.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise planning presentation choices from purpose and audience through final revision.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise planning presentation choices from purpose and audience through final revision.
lessonContent: A strong presentation starts with audience and purpose.
The speaker should choose main points that fit the purpose.
Notes should guide the speaker without becoming a script to read word for word.
Visual aids should make ideas clearer for the audience.
Practising helps the speaker check timing, clarity, voice, and confidence.
practiceIdeas: Share the student mission for practice stars.

Review missed questions before assigning the next Oral Communication and Presentation lesson.

studentActivityPlan.title: Presentation Prep Mission
studentActivityPlan.description: Choose preparation steps that make a presentation clear and ready.
studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.title: Preparing a Presentation Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Audience, purpose, main points, notes, visuals, practice, timing, and final checks

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity for guided speaking and listening decisions and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Presentation Prep Mission
studentActivity.mission: Choose preparation steps that make a presentation clear and ready.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: preparation starts early
steps.text: A presentation is easier to give when the speaker knows the audience, purpose, main points, and support before making slides or notes.

steps.title: Audience and Purpose
steps.prompt: Decide what listeners need
steps.text: Audience and purpose guide almost every choice. A talk for classmates may use different examples than a talk for parents or younger students.

steps.title: Audience
steps.prompt: A student is presenting to Grade 2 students about playground safety. Which choice best fits the audience?
choices: use simple examples from recess routines
include a detailed report about school policy
compare several playground designs from different schools
steps.correctAnswer: use simple examples from recess routines
steps.feedback: Correct. The examples fit younger listeners.
steps.hint: Choose what the audience can use.

steps.title: Purpose
steps.prompt: A presentation is meant to teach classmates how to check a source. Which main point belongs?
choices: Look for the author, date, and evidence before trusting information.
Websites can use menus, images, and search boxes.
Some students prefer doing research with a partner.
steps.correctAnswer: Look for the author, date, and evidence before trusting information.
steps.feedback: Yes. It fits the teaching purpose.
steps.hint: Choose the point that matches the goal.

steps.title: Main Points
steps.prompt: Which plan is strongest for a short presentation about a favourite Canadian animal?
choices: habitat, diet, adaptations, and one interesting fact
animal name, poster colour, project partner, and font choice
book title, class period, drawing size, and presentation day
steps.correctAnswer: habitat, diet, adaptations, and one interesting fact
steps.feedback: Correct. The points fit the topic.
steps.hint: Main points should help the audience learn.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Audience and purpose should guide presentation choices.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. They shape content, wording, and visuals.
steps.hint: Planning begins with audience and purpose.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised planning presentation choices.

steps.title: Check Before Sharing
steps.prompt: Preparation includes practice
steps.text: Practising helps a speaker notice unclear parts, timing problems, missing support, or visual aids that are hard to read.

steps.title: Notes
steps.prompt: Which note style would best support a student during a presentation?
choices: short cue words for each main point and key example
full paragraphs to read from the page
only the title and the final sentence
steps.correctAnswer: short cue words for each main point and key example
steps.feedback: Correct. Cue words help the speaker speak naturally.
steps.hint: Notes should guide, not replace speaking.

steps.title: Visual Aid
steps.prompt: Which visual aid best supports a talk comparing two habitats?
choices: a simple labelled chart showing key similarities and differences
a large decorative title with small facts below
a photo that looks interesting but is not explained
steps.correctAnswer: a simple labelled chart showing key similarities and differences
steps.feedback: Yes. It helps the audience compare.
steps.hint: Visuals should make ideas clearer.

steps.title: Practice Check
steps.prompt: What should a student check while practising a presentation?
choices: timing, clear voice, order of ideas, and hard words
whether every slide uses the same number of words
whether the longest section comes first
steps.correctAnswer: timing, clear voice, order of ideas, and hard words
steps.feedback: Correct. Those checks improve delivery.
steps.hint: Practice helps find problems before presenting.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A speaker can revise a presentation after practising it.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Practice often shows what needs revision.
steps.hint: Practise, notice, revise.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised preparing a presentation.

questions.prompt: A talk is for younger students learning library routines. Which choice fits best?
choices: simple steps with familiar school examples
a long explanation of library classification
a comparison of several research databases
questions.correctAnswer: simple steps with familiar school examples
questions.reviewNote: The audience needs clear, familiar examples.

questions.prompt: A presentation is meant to persuade classmates to join a cleanup team. Which point belongs?
choices: The team helps keep shared spaces ready for everyone.
The sign-up sheet is printed on white paper.
The classroom has several recycling containers.
questions.correctAnswer: The team helps keep shared spaces ready for everyone.

questions.prompt: Which set of main points fits a presentation about a book character?
choices: goal, challenge, important choice, and how the character changes
cover colour, chapter count, page numbers, and font size
author name, library shelf, due date, and reading spot
questions.correctAnswer: goal, challenge, important choice, and how the character changes
questions.reviewNote: Those points help explain a character.

questions.prompt: Which notes are best for speaking naturally?
choices: cue words and key examples
full paragraphs to read word for word
only the opening sentence
questions.correctAnswer: cue words and key examples

questions.prompt: Which visual aid best supports a presentation about a process?
choices: a labelled sequence chart
a background picture with small text
a title page with no details
questions.correctAnswer: a labelled sequence chart
questions.reviewNote: A sequence chart shows process order.

questions.prompt: Why practise before presenting?
choices: to check timing, clarity, and order
to memorize every possible audience question
to make the presentation longer
questions.correctAnswer: to check timing, clarity, and order

questions.prompt: Visual aids should support the message, not distract from it.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: A presentation plan should begin with audience and purpose.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.reviewNote: Audience and purpose guide the plan.

lessons.title: Unit 6 Final Quiz
lessons.teacherOverview: Use this quiz after students complete the Oral Communication and Presentation lessons.
lessons.teacherSummary: The Unit 6 final quiz checks active listening, good questions, clear speaking, short talk organization, voice and body language, group discussion, feedback, and presentation preparation.

quiz.title: Oral Communication and Presentation Unit Quiz

questions.prompt: A speaker says, 'Our group tested three materials. The felt kept the ice cold longest.' What is the main idea?
choices: The test showed felt worked best as an insulator.
The group used three materials in a test.
The speaker used ice during the investigation.
questions.correctAnswer: The test showed felt worked best as an insulator.
questions.reviewNote: The main idea explains what the test showed.

questions.prompt: Which question best clarifies an unclear word?
choices: What do you mean by 'conclusion' in this investigation?
Which slide has your chart on it?
How long did your group practise?
questions.correctAnswer: What do you mean by 'conclusion' in this investigation?
questions.reviewNote: It asks for the meaning of the unclear word.

questions.prompt: Which response shows active listening?
choices: So your evidence is that the character changes after chapter four.
I chose a different book for my project.
Your presentation had five slides.
questions.correctAnswer: So your evidence is that the character changes after chapter four.
questions.reviewNote: It connects to the speaker's idea.

questions.prompt: Which question asks for evidence?
choices: Which fact from your source supports that claim?
How many pictures did your source include?
Did you find the source yesterday?
questions.correctAnswer: Which fact from your source supports that claim?

questions.prompt: A speaker says, 'The second design was stronger.' Which follow-up question fits?
choices: What change made the second design stronger?
Which colour was the first design?
Who carried the materials to the table?
questions.correctAnswer: What change made the second design stronger?
questions.reviewNote: It builds on the speaker's statement.

questions.prompt: Which voice choice helps in a classroom presentation?
choices: speak loudly enough for the audience to hear comfortably
use the same quiet voice as a partner talk
make only the introduction louder
questions.correctAnswer: speak loudly enough for the audience to hear comfortably

questions.prompt: What should a speaker do when listeners seem to miss key points?
choices: slow down and pause after important ideas
add more details before moving on
read the rest from notes without stopping
questions.correctAnswer: slow down and pause after important ideas

questions.prompt: Which opening is strongest?
choices: Today I will explain how three safety habits help during science investigations.
Science investigations can use several kinds of materials.
My presentation has a title and a conclusion.
questions.correctAnswer: Today I will explain how three safety habits help during science investigations.

questions.prompt: Which phrase signals a final summary?
choices: To sum up
For example
Another reason
questions.correctAnswer: To sum up

questions.prompt: Which sentence supports the point 'Practice improves a presentation'?
choices: Practice helps a speaker notice unclear words and timing problems.
Practice can happen at a desk or in front of a mirror.
Some students practise during the morning.
questions.correctAnswer: Practice helps a speaker notice unclear words and timing problems.

questions.prompt: Which tone fits a serious safety reminder?
choices: calm and clear
playful and dramatic
uncertain and rushed
questions.correctAnswer: calm and clear

questions.prompt: Which gesture best supports explaining three steps?
choices: briefly count the steps with fingers
hold notes higher each time
move to a new spot for every sentence
questions.correctAnswer: briefly count the steps with fingers

questions.prompt: Which sentence builds on another student's idea?
choices: I agree, and the chart gives another example of that pattern.
I want to talk about a different part now.
I wrote down the same answer earlier.
questions.correctAnswer: I agree, and the chart gives another example of that pattern.
questions.reviewNote: It adds support to the idea.

questions.prompt: Which response gives a different opinion respectfully?
choices: I read the evidence differently because the last sentence changes the meaning.
Our group should use my answer instead.
That idea is not the one I wrote down.
questions.correctAnswer: I read the evidence differently because the last sentence changes the meaning.

questions.prompt: Which feedback is most useful?
choices: Your main idea is clear; add one example to support your second point.
Your presentation is nice and has good parts.
You should change the part in the middle.
questions.correctAnswer: Your main idea is clear; add one example to support your second point.

questions.prompt: Feedback says, 'Your facts are strong, but the order is hard to follow.' What should the student revise?
choices: organize the facts in a clearer order
replace the facts with shorter ones
change the title and leave the facts
questions.correctAnswer: organize the facts in a clearer order

questions.prompt: A talk is for younger students. Which choice fits best?
choices: use simple examples they already understand
include technical terms from older grades
focus mainly on how the slideshow was made
questions.correctAnswer: use simple examples they already understand
questions.reviewNote: Audience affects word choice and examples.

questions.prompt: Which notes best support natural speaking?
choices: cue words for main points and examples
full paragraphs to read word for word
only the title and closing sentence
questions.correctAnswer: cue words for main points and examples

questions.prompt: A strong oral response should connect to what the speaker said.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: A visual aid should make the message easier for the audience to understand.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.reviewNote: Visual aids should support the message.

unitGradePlan.note: Final Oral Communication and Presentation mark recommendation: 60% unit quiz and 40% average of lesson quizzes.

unitAssessmentPlan.lessonQuizzes: Each lesson has a short scored quiz to check the lesson focus.
unitAssessmentPlan.unitTest: The final unit quiz checks active listening, good questions, clear speaking, short talk organization, voice and body language, group discussion, feedback, and presentation preparation.
